title.title: The critical dimension of the one-phase Bernoulli problem is 7
title.subtitle: Claim: every one-homogeneous minimizer in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d \le 6$, is flat, so free boundaries are smooth through dimension 6

plain: A boundary that settles where energy is least, like a soap film: up to which dimension must it be smooth?

object.axisLabel: $d^*$: the first dimension with a nonflat minimizing cone

beats.text: Free boundaries are smooth away from a singular set governed by $d^*$
The claim: no nonflat cone in dimensions 5 and 6, so $d^* = 7$

steps: Suppose a nonflat minimizing cone exists in dimension 5 or 6
Pair a Hessian test with a field whose divergence beats its energy
Exact certificates check the inequality: the cone must be flat

data.smaller: a test that lowers its energy

achievement.label: The critical dimension of the one-phase Bernoulli problem
achievement.note: The Bernoulli analogue of Simons' theorem for minimal surfaces

verify.detail: Lean: only the nonflat cone in $\mathbb{R}^7$, the 2009 half. Flatness in $d = 5, 6$ is not formalized
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean docs; we did not build the Lean

voice.text: Free boundaries can have singular points. The critical dimension was known: five, six or seven.
A stability test, checked by exact certificates, flattens every cone below dimension seven.
Claimed: the critical dimension is seven.

sources.quote: Caffarelli–Jerison–Kenig 2004: d*≥4; Jerison–Savin 2015: stable homogeneous cones flat for d≤4, so d*≥5; De Silva–Jerison 2009: nonflat minimizing cone in R^7, so d*≤7.

sources.quote: Family 367 claims $d^* = 7$. It is the free-boundary analogue of Simons' theorem that makes 8 critical for minimal surfaces.
